Automotive, machinery, consumer goods, electrical equipment and business services are driving the UK–Romania economic relationship, with bilateral trade reaching £10.3 billion in the four quarters to the end of Q4 2025, up 4.9% year-on-year, according to the latest data released by the UK Department for Business and Trade. UK exports to Romania increased by 7.0% to £3.0 billion, while UK imports from Romania rose by 4.0% to £7.3 billion, positioning Romania as the UK’s 32nd-largest trading partner. UK–Romania economic relationship Trade in goods remains anchored by strong industrial and manufacturing activity. Cars were the UK’s largest goods import from Romania, reaching £1.3 billion and accounting for 30.4% of total goods imports from the country, following an 18.4% year-on-year increase. Other leading categories included beverages and tobacco, general industrial machinery and electrical goods. UK goods exports to Romania were led by beverages and tobacco, mechanical power generators and cars, highlighting the importance of established industrial supply chains and the potential for further sector-specific cooperation. Services are also becoming an increasingly important component of the bilateral relationship. UK services exports to Romania increased by 16.1%, reaching £1.5 billion and accounting for 50.5% of total UK exports to the country. Travel was the largest service category, representing 37.1% of UK services exports to Romania and 43.2% of UK services imports from Romania, followed by other business services and transportation. The significant contribution of business services reflects the growing sophistication of bilateral trade and creates further opportunities in professional services, technology, research and development, management consulting and digitalisation. Commenting on the latest data, Robert Uzună, Chairman of BRCC, stated : “The latest figures mark another increase in UK–Romania bilateral trade, confirming the positive momentum of the economic relationship. Particularly encouraging is the strength of key sectors such as automotive, machinery and electrical equipment, together with the increasing relevance of business services. These results provide a solid foundation for further development and point to new opportunities for investment, innovation and sector-specific partnerships. At BRCC, we will continue to connect companies, institutions and industry leaders, helping transform this momentum into concrete projects and sustainable long-term growth.” Robert Uzună, Chairman of the BRCC. As a central facilitator of this relationship, the British Romanian Chamber of Commerce (BRCC) continues to play a key role in building and sustaining a strong bilateral business ecosystem. Through its network of members, strategic partnerships and ongoing dialogue with public authorities in both countries, BRCC supports companies in identifying sector-specific opportunities, fostering relevant connections and developing new avenues for growth. Key fields of cooperation and further potential Beyond trade, investment flows highlight both progress and untapped potential. The stock of UK foreign direct investment in Romania stood at £752 million at the end of 2024, decreasing by 19.9% compared with the previous year and signalling an opportunity to strengthen investment pipelines and long-term capital engagement. In contrast, Romanian foreign direct investment in the UK increased by 22.2%, reaching £303 million, reflecting increased confidence and the continued international expansion of Romanian businesses. Romania’s broader economic trajectory reinforces its growing importance in the European landscape. Its GDP is projected to reach $480.8 billion in 2026, positioning the country as the world’s 39th-largest economy. Exporting activity was estimated to support approximately 2.6 million jobs in Romania in 2022, including around 103,600 jobs supported by exports to the UK. The UK’s overall market share in Romania stood at 2.2% in 2024, indicating further room for expansion, particularly in automotive, advanced manufacturing, industrial machinery, electrical equipment, business services and technology. The combination of established industrial supply chains and a growing services component provides a strong foundation for a deeper and more integrated economic relationship between Romania and the United Kingdom. About British Romanian Chamber of Commerce The British Romanian Chamber of Commerce is the premier business-led organisation promoting bilateral trade and investment between the United Kingdom and Romania. Our mission is to facilitate and increase trade between those two countries through business-to-business dialogue. The British Romanian Chamber of Commerce plays an influential role in creating and sustaining an environment in which free-trade and investment flourishes. Through the facilitation of partnerships, and with an extensive network of influential corporate and individual members, the British Romanian Chamber of Commerce provides the resource, knowledge and infrastructure support vital to UK companies to make the most of emerging opportunities in Romania, and for Romanian companies to do business in the established markets of the UK. Established in 1998, the BRCC is an independent organisation, owned entirely by its members, with offices in London, Bucharest, Cluj and Timisoara. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/14/turk.text: Turkish Airlines has permanently axed its Luanda route, the latest in a series of international carriers to drop the Angolan capital since Angola inaugurated its new airport in 2023.The Istanbul-based carrier removed Luanda from its future schedule earlier this month, along with Juba, Kinshasa, Libreville and Lusaka, after those services had been suspended through 24 October.Turkish Airlines initially described the suspension as temporary when it announced the move in April, citing fuel costs.It had operated a triangular service through Kinshasa rather than a direct connection, but the route gave Luanda passengers onward access to destinations across Europe, Asia and beyond via Istanbul.Brussels Airlines ended its Luanda service on 25 March 2025 as part of a restructuring within the Lufthansa Group, redirecting passengers onto Lufthansa's direct Frankfurt–Luanda flights.TAAG Angola Airlines suspended its Madrid route — codeshared with Iberia — in January 2024 and later removed a planned return from its schedule.Iberia never reversed its decision to suspend flights to Luanda, in place since 2016, opting instead to codeshare with TAAG since 2022. That link is now gone as well.South African Airways (SAA) also only places its code on TAAG-operated flights.Low passenger numbers plague new airportThe departures come as Angola's Dr António Agostinho Neto International Airport, about 45km from central Luanda, struggles to establish itself as the regional hub the government promised when it inaugurated the facility in November 2023.Built by Chinese state-owned company AVIC and designed for a maximum annual capacity of 15 million passengers, the airport handled 756,028 passengers in all of 2025, according to figures from the airport's temporary operator ATO.By 24 February of this year, total passenger numbers since the first domestic flight in November 2024 stood at 1,090,861, including 444,212 international passengers.The full transfer of services from the old Quatro de Fevereiro airport was completed on 1 March — more than two years after the inauguration — when South African carrier Airlink moved its Johannesburg flights to the new facility.In December 2025, ATO's Director of Planning and Quality Vissolela Chivunda said the airport expected around 4 million passengers in 2026.Luanda remains served by TAP Air Portugal, Air France, Lufthansa, Royal Air Maroc, Ethiopian Airlines, Qatar Airways, Airlink and TAAG, alongside Compagnie Africaine d'Aviation, which began two weekly flights from Kinshasa on 21 August.

https://www.thestar.com.my/lifestyle/liv.text: Living A red hot issue: Hungary's paprika producers battle to save the signature spice By AGENCY Photos By ATTILA KISBENEDEK/AFP Wednesday, 14 Oct 2026 | 12:00 PM MYT share bookmark Related Stories Wellness 15h ago Junk food linked to ‘silent stroke’ Nation 1d ago Agriculture and Food Security Ministry stepping up prep for Super El Nino Nation 25 Oct 2026 Sabah’s agro-food sector can be widened further The Paprika and Gastronomy Festival in Kalocsa highlights local ground paprika and the culinary traditions associated with it. Working from before dawn until midnight, farmers Nikoletta Pajsan Nagy and Laszlo Pajsan fought Europe's driest summer ever to save their red pepper harvest in Hungary. Unable to irrigate much of their 2.5ha land because power lines run across it, they repeatedly loosened the soil around the plants, which are used to make the central European country's signature spice, paprika. "I was absolutely convinced that we'd have to take on part-time jobs because they'd burn out," said Pajsan Nagy, 44, while selling her family's products at the annual town fair –Paprika and Gastronomy Festival – in Kalocsa, in southern Hungary. "But somehow the crop turned out bigger and more beautiful than in previous years. It was a miracle," she said, recalling some 20-hour days in the field. The couple see themselves as a dwindling profession, as cultivation of paprika – an indispensable ingredient in traditional cuisine – has declined over the past several decades in Hungary, with many small producers going out of business. Nets with paprika hanging from the roof of the home of a local producer in Homokmegy, Hungary. Squeezing producers The area devoted to paprika peaked at 13,029ha in 1979 and had fallen to 1,410ha by 2024, according to official statistics. While cheap imports from China and parts of South America are squeezing producers, climate change is making paprika production more difficult and costly, according to Robert Braj, an adviser at Dutch-owned BWA Kft, one of Hungary's top food-seasoning manufacturers. "There are longer droughts, more extreme heatwaves, while new pests and diseases are spreading," said Braj. Along with some other European Union nations, Hungary experienced its driest summer since records began in 1901 and its second-hottest on record, according to national weather service HungaroMet. Labour shortages are also a problem. At the annual fair, paprika seller Agnes Toth recalled picking up peppers as a child, taking part in the family business. "Back then, we grew paprika on 6ha. Now it's around 3ha because there aren't enough seasonal workers to harvest it by hand," said Toth, 44. "A family couldn't make a living from this any more... Everyone has a full-time job. I'm a teacher, my brother is a firefighter," she said. Farmer Rozsa Benyi holding up two packages of ground paprika at her home in Homokmegy. Paprika cultivation and the production of traditional paprika strings are still important in Hungary today. Hungary's Agriculture and Food Economy Ministry said it seeks to strengthen producers' competitiveness, but it is yet to announce any new measures. At the fair last month in Kalocsa, one of Hungary's main paprika-growing regions, the aroma of meat stews and fish soups laced with the vibrant scarlet spice filled the air as teams poured generous amounts into their cauldrons at a cooking contest. "For us Hungarians, paprika is a wonder," one of the competitors, local fast-food restaurant owner Imre Zseni said, while stirring a beef stew. Booths were adorned with strings of dried red peppers – the raw ingredient used to make paprika – recalling a sight once common on houses in the surrounding countryside every autumn. Originating from the Americas, peppers found their way to Hungary's sun-drenched, fertile river plains around Kalocsa and Szeged in the 16th century. The two historic paprika-production centres are now recognised with the EU's protected designation of origin status. Ethnographer Imre Romsics said paprika became an important symbol of Hungarian identity during the 19th century, "alongside costume, folk art and other traditions". But younger generations cook fewer traditional Hungarian recipes, and they prefer food "that is faster and easier to prepare", according to specialist Braj. – AFP Follow us on our official WhatsApp channel for breaking news alerts and key updates!
